summary: Defines an SMTP submission extension that lets a client ask the server to hold a message and release it for delivery at a future time. This is helpful to clients that cannot keep the message themselves until the appointed time. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: You drop a letter at the post office and say, do not send this until Friday. The post office keeps it and sends it for you at the right time.

questions: how to schedule email delivery with smtp
what is the smtp future message release extension
what is the maximum future release interval
subtitle: How a mail client can ask its submission server to hold a message and release it at a later time.

tldr.problem: Some mail clients have no local storage or cannot act at an appointed time, yet users want to compose a message now and have it delivered later.
tldr.mechanism: The submission server advertises a FUTURERELEASE keyword in its EHLO reply, and the client adds either a HOLDFOR interval or a HOLDUNTIL date-time to the MAIL command so the server queues the message until then.
tldr.outcome: The server stores the message and must not release it early. Per-user quotas guard its storage, and the Date header is not hidden, so recipients can still see the delay.

today: RFC 4865 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2007. It has not been obsoleted and no later RFC is recorded as updating it. It updates RFC 3463 and RFC 3464, adding two enhanced status codes and the Future-Release-Request DSN field.

sections.title: Why Hold a Message
sections.content:
RFC 4865 defines an extension to the SMTP submission protocol that lets a client say when a message should be released for delivery. The RFC notes that composing a message now and sending it later is a widely used feature in the voice messaging community. Its examples are announcements to be heard at the start of a work day, birthday greetings sent a day or so ahead, and a lightweight personal reminder service.

The extension lets a client use server-based storage for a message that should wait in queue until an appointed time. This helps clients that do not have local storage or are otherwise unable to release a message at the right moment.
sections.eli5: Sometimes you write a note today but want it read tomorrow. This lets the mail helper hold it for you until the right time.

sections.title: The FUTURERELEASE Extension
sections.content:
The extension is called Future Message Release and uses the normal SMTP service extension mechanism. Its Extended Hello (EHLO) keyword is FUTURERELEASE. The server (the message submission agent, or MSA) follows the keyword with two required values separated by spaces: max-future-release-interval and max-future-release-date-time.

The interval is a positive integer of seconds, in the range 1 to 999999999, that is the longest time the MSA will hold messages. The date-time is a UTC timestamp for the most remote moment until which it will hold them. A reply line looks like 250-FUTURERELEASE followed by the interval and the date-time.

The extension adds no new SMTP verbs. It is appropriate only for the submission protocol and not for standard SMTP, and a possible hold parameter lengthens the maximum MAIL command by 34 characters.
sections.eli5: The mail helper tells you up front how long it is willing to keep a letter, both as a number of seconds and as a latest date.

sections.title: HOLDFOR and HOLDUNTIL
sections.content:
To ask for a delayed release, the client adds exactly one hold parameter to the MAIL command. HOLDFOR= carries an interval in seconds: how long the MSA holds the message before release. HOLDUNTIL= carries a UTC date-time: the moment until which the message is held.

Having two ways to say the same thing is called unfortunate by the RFC itself. It exists because some clients have an accurate clock but no time zone, and others have no accurate clock at all, so likely only one of the two works for them. The RFC expects servers to have accurate time and to convert easily between the two. Leaving the parameter off does not imply a default value.
sections.eli5: You can say wait two days or wait until Friday noon. Some devices only know how to say one of those, so both are allowed.

sections.title: Client and Server Duties
sections.content:
A client MUST first verify that the MSA supports the extension, and MUST include one, and only one, hold parameter. With HOLDFOR the interval must be at most the advertised maximum interval. With HOLDUNTIL the date-time must be no later than the advertised maximum date-time.

An MSA MUST comply with the base submission protocol and MUST NOT advertise FUTURERELEASE on any port other than the submission port. It MUST accept a valid hold parameter on an otherwise correct MAIL command and MUST NOT release the message before the interval elapses or the date-time arrives.

It MUST reject a MAIL command whose value exceeds the advertised maximum, is otherwise invalid, or that contains more than one hold parameter. When rejecting, it SHOULD reply with code 501 and enhanced status code 5.5.4.
sections.eli5: The rules are like a babysitter agreement: ask for only one waiting time, do not ask for longer than allowed, and the helper must not send early.

sections.title: Interaction with Other Extensions
sections.content:
Delivery Status Notifications (DSNs) and Message Disposition Notifications (MDNs) are reports about messages, so a client MUST NOT request future release when sending either to the MSA. If the MSA generates a DSN for a held message, it MUST include an Arrival-Date field and a new Future-Release-Request field in the machine-readable part. That field repeats the original request as for; followed by an interval or until; followed by a date-time.

The Deliver By extension sets a deadline for delivery, which could clash with a longer hold. A client using both MUST make the deliver-by time farther in the future than the release time, and the MSA MUST reject the MAIL command if the release time is farther out than the deliver-by time. It SHOULD use code 501 and status 5.5.4.
sections.eli5: If you also say deliver this by Thursday, you cannot tell the helper to hold it until Friday. The helper will say no, because both cannot be true.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Held messages use up server storage, so the RFC lists several risks. Unauthorized future-release messages could overwhelm an MSA's storage, and the authorization already required by base submission is expected to defend against this. Even authorized use could do so without limits, so an MSA's future-release storage SHOULD be subject to a per-user quota. If a message would exceed the quota, the MSA MUST reject the MAIL command, and SHOULD reply with code 552.

The RFC defines two new enhanced status codes for this: X.7.16 (per-user quota exceeded, try again after the queue drains) and X.7.17 (system quota exceeded). A wrong clock on the MSA can cause early or late release, because both mechanisms depend on it.

The extension also involves some deception: delivery is deliberately later than it otherwise would be, and nothing hides this. The Date header is unchanged after submission, though a client MAY put the release time there, and trace fields like Received are not required to be altered.
sections.eli5: If anyone could leave unlimited letters at the post office, it would fill up. So each person gets a limit, and the post office does not hide that a letter was held back.
